lesson.title: The Power to Detect What's Really There
lesson.summary: Power is the probability that a hypothesis test correctly rejects a false null hypothesis, and it tells you how good your test actually is at catching a real effect.
lesson.body:
Every hypothesis test can fail in two ways. A Type I error rejects a true null hypothesis, and its probability is the significance level, alpha, that you choose before collecting data. A Type II error is the opposite mistake: failing to reject a false null hypothesis, missing a real effect that is actually there. The probability of a Type II error is called beta. Power is defined as 1 minus beta, the probability that the test correctly rejects a false null hypothesis when a specific alternative value of the parameter is true. In plain language, power measures how good a test is at finding an effect that genuinely exists.

Power is not a single fixed number for a test. It depends on which specific true value of the parameter you assume, how far that true value is from the null hypothesis, the sample size, the variability in the population, and the significance level alpha you chose. Because of this, power calculations always start with a specific alternative scenario: if the true mean were actually this value, what is the chance my test would catch it. A test can have high power against a large true effect and low power against a small one, using the exact same data collection plan.

Here is a concrete illustration. Suppose a null hypothesis claims a population mean is mu0 = 80, tested against Ha: mu > 80, using alpha = 0.05, with a known population standard deviation sigma = 15 and a sample size n = 36. The standard error of the sample mean is 15 divided by the square root of 36, which is 15/6 = 2.5. Because this is a one-sided upper-tail test at alpha = 0.05, the critical z-value is 1.645, so the test rejects H0 whenever the sample mean exceeds 80 + 1.645(2.5) = 84.11. Now ask: what is the power of this test if the true population mean is actually 88. Standardize the critical value 84.11 using the true sampling distribution, which is centered at 88 with the same standard error 2.5: z = (84.11 - 88) / 2.5 = -1.56. Power is the probability of landing above the critical value under this true distribution, which is P(Z > -1.56) = 0.94. So there is about a 94 percent chance this test correctly detects a true mean of 88, and correspondingly about a 6 percent chance, beta, that it fails to, even though the effect is real.

This calculation also shows exactly why power matters when you are designing a study, not just analyzing one after the fact. A test with low power can leave a real, important effect statistically undetected, not because the effect is not real but because the study was not sensitive enough to see it. The next section looks at exactly which choices, sample size, effect size, variability, and alpha, push power up or down, so you can build studies that have a reasonable chance of catching what you are looking for.
